reasoning: Quote is verbatim (ms3/A3_AUDIO_COMPANION_QUIZZES.md line 3836) and is the feedback attached to the distractor 'The serotonergic system via 5-HT2A receptors' in AR-02 Q2. The problem is real: the feedback tells the learner that 5-HT2A receptor action 'describes the mechanism of most traditional SSRIs,' which is wrong pharmacology — SSRIs act by inhibiting the serotonin transporter (SERT), while 5-HT2A agonism is the mechanism of classic serotonergic psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD). This SSRI-vs-psychedelic mechanism distinction is exactly what MS3s are tested on, so the string actively misteaches. Nothing in the surrounding quiz corrects it. The replacement cleanly separates the two mechanisms (psychedelics = 5-HT2A agonism; SSRIs = SERT blockade) and correctly ties back to ketamine's NMDA mechanism, at an appropriate MS3 level.

Quote is verbatim (ms3/A3_AUDIO_COMPANION_QUIZZES.md line 3383), attached to the distractor 'Neither monotherapy was superior to placebo' in AR-08 Q2. Verified against the POTS abstract retrieved from PubMed (JAMA 2004, PMID 15507582, DOI https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.292.16.1969): on the primary CY-BOCS outcome all three active arms beat placebo (sertraline alone P=.007), but on the remission outcome 'CBT alone ... did differ from placebo (P = .002), whereas sertraline alone did not (P = .10)', with remission rates 39.3% (CBT), 21.4% (sertraline), 3.6% (placebo). So the feedback's claim that BOTH monotherapies had significantly higher remission rates than placebo mis-states the trial's remission analysis precisely as the finding alleges, and the finding's numbers all match the paper. The replacement states the primary-outcome superiority and the remission nuance exactly as the abstract reports them and is level-appropriate; the finding's 'medium' confidence can be raised to high now that the paper has been checked.
